texts.orig: 2.1 ACTESTS

texts.label: text
texts.orig: AC Tests are tests performed by the manufacturer to determine cable insulation integrity. The applied ac voltage is used as a pass/fail test. AC tests have seldom been performed in the field. (See Section 13.)

texts.orig: 2.2 ACCEPTANCE TESTING
texts.text: 2.2 ACCEPTANCE TESTING

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Acceptance testing is performed by the user upon receipt of new cable and connection devices to confirm that no damage occurred during shipping and handling. (See Section 7.)

texts.orig: 2.3 CONDUCTOR RESISTANCE
texts.text: 2.3 CONDUCTOR RESISTANCE

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Conductor Resistance is that property of the conductor that resists the flow of electrons (direct current). It is affected by conductor cross-sectional area, conductor length, conductor material, and conductor temperature.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 2.4 CONNECTORS
texts.text: 2.4 CONNECTORS

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Connectors are attachments for electrically conducting power through the wellhead and đownhole packer. These devices consist of two separable components which complete the electrical circuit when mated.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 2.5  DC TESTS
texts.text: 2.5  DC TESTS

texts.label: text
texts.orig: DC Tests are tests performed by the manufacturer or user to determine insulation integrity. The applied dc voltage may be used as a pass/fail test. The leakage current of the applied voltage may be used as a comparative measure of cable system quality. (See Section 12.)

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 2.6 DIAGNOSTIC TESTING
texts.text: 2.6 DIAGNOSTIC TESTING

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Diagnostic Testing is performed to locate faults, determine the cause of failure, and evaluate the condition of used cable after faults have been located and repaired. These tests may also be used to help determine suitability for reuse. (See Section 10.)
texts.text: Diagnostic Testing is performed to locate faults, determine the cause of failure, and evaluate the condition of used cable after faults have been located and repaired. These tests may also be used to help determine suitability for reuse. (See Section 10.)

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 2.7 GROUNDING STICK (DISCHARGE RESISTOR)
texts.text: 2.7 GROUNDING STICK (DISCHARGE RESISTOR)

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A grounding stick should be used to discharge a cable after testing. A grounding stick is an assembly with a resistance not less than 10,000 ohm/kV of test voltage.
texts.text: A grounding stick should be used to discharge a cable after testing. A grounding stick is an assembly with a resistance not less than 10,000 ohm/kV of test voltage.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 2.8 HIGH POTENTIAL (HI-POT) TESTS
texts.text: 2.8 HIGH POTENTIAL (HI-POT) TESTS

texts.label: text
texts.orig: High potential insulation tests are intended to provide nondestructive ac or dc strength testing of insulation. A dc test is considered high potential when it is conducted at a voltage level two times the insulation rating plus 1000 volts or more. An ac test is considered high potential when it is conducted at a voltage level greater than 1.2 times the insulation rating.
texts.text: High potential insulation tests are intended to provide nondestructive ac or dc strength testing of insulation. A dc test is considered high potential when it is conducted at a voltage level two times the insulation rating plus 1000 volts or more. An ac test is considered high potential when it is conducted at a voltage level greater than 1.2 times the insulation rating.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The tests may be leakage current tests or voltage withstand tests. Direct current high potential tests are widely used for acceptance and maintenance (proof) testing.
texts.text: The tests may be leakage current tests or voltage withstand tests. Direct current high potential tests are widely used for acceptance and maintenance (proof) testing.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Insulation conductance is equivalent to the reciprocal of insulation resistance. It is usually measured in units of μa/1000 V/1000 ft.

texts.orig: 2.10 INSULATION IMPEDANCE
texts.text: 2.10 INSULATION IMPEDANCE

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Insulation impedance is an electrical measurement of the opposition to the flow of alternating current through the insulation. Impedance includes resistance and alternating current effects. Changes in impedance may be caused by imperfections in or deformations of the insulation.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 2.11 INSULATION RESISTANCE
texts.text: 2.11 INSULATION RESISTANCE

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Insulation Resistance (IR) is a property of the insulation that opposes the flow of direct current through the insulation. (See Section 11.)
texts.text: Insulation Resistance (IR) is a property of the insulation that opposes the flow of direct current through the insulation. (See Section 11.)

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 2.12 IR TESTS
texts.text: 2.12 IR TESTS

texts.label: text
texts.orig: IR Tests are conducted by impressing a dc voltage across the insulation. This will produce a leakage current through the insulation. The ratio of impressed voltage to leakage current is insulation resistance. This test uses a megohmmeter. (See Section 11.)
texts.text: IR Tests are conducted by impressing a dc voltage across the insulation. This will produce a leakage current through the insulation. The ratio of impressed voltage to leakage current is insulation resistance. This test uses a megohmmeter. (See Section 11.)

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 2.13 LEAKAGE CURRENT
texts.text: 2.13 LEAKAGE CURRENT

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Leakage Current is the current reading resulting from conduction through an insulating medium or over surfaces such as terminations. This current is usually measured in microamps.
texts.text: Leakage Current is the current reading resulting from conduction through an insulating medium or over surfaces such as terminations. This current is usually measured in microamps.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 4.1 DESCRIPTION
texts.text: 4.1 DESCRIPTION

texts.label: text
texts.orig: High direct-voltage testing of cable systems involves all of the hazards normally associated with working on energized circuits, as well as several unique hazards that should be addressed.
texts.text: High direct-voltage testing of cable systems involves all of the hazards normally associated with working on energized circuits, as well as several unique hazards that should be addressed.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 4.2 APPLICATION
texts.text: 4.2 APPLICATION

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Cables can hold a dc electrical charge for long periods of time after voltage has been removed. Electrical charge is maintained because of high capacitance and dielectric absorption characteristics of the insulation. For this reason proper grounding procedures should be followed to eliminate personnel hazards.
texts.text: Cables can hold a dc electrical charge for long periods of time after voltage has been removed. Electrical charge is maintained because of high capacitance and dielectric absorption characteristics of the insulation. For this reason proper grounding procedures should be followed to eliminate personnel hazards.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Furthermore, cable subjected to high-voltage dc testing that is not properly grounded following the test can have dangerous charge buildup. This buildup is a characteristic of all insulating materials.
texts.text: Furthermore, cable subjected to high-voltage dc testing that is not properly grounded following the test can have dangerous charge buildup. This buildup is a characteristic of all insulating materials.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 4.3 PROCEDURES
texts.text: 4.3 PROCEDURES

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Cable circuits will normally have one or more ends remote from the location of the test equipment and test operator. These ends should be cleared and guarded to ensure the safety of personnel. Reliable voice communication should be established between all such locations and the test operator.
texts.text: Cable circuits will normally have one or more ends remote from the location of the test equipment and test operator. texts.label: text
texts.orig: All ends as well as all connecting leads of components being tested require guarding from accidental contact by such means as barriers, enclosures, or a watchman at all points. The ends require separation from all elements not to be subjected to test and by a distance of not less than 6 in.

texts.label: text

The only time a ground connection should be removed is when test voltage is being applied to that conductor.

texts.orig: 5 Visual Inspection
texts.text: 5 Visual Inspection

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 5.1 DESCRIPTION
texts.text: 5.1 DESCRIPTION

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This procedure involves the visual inspection of a cable system prior to and following electrical testing. The procedure is appropriate for all tests covered in the recommended practice. As part of the procedure, the cable will be spooled to another reel. Then the cable should be re-spooled in its original armor direction.
texts.text: This procedure involves the visual inspection of a cable system prior to and following electrical testing. The procedure is appropriate for all tests covered in the recommended practice. As part of the procedure, the cable will be spooled to another reel. Then the cable should be re-spooled in its original armor direction.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 5.2 APPLICATION
texts.text: 5.2 APPLICATION

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The first application is to detect physical damage or deterioration that requires corrective action before electrical testing. A second application is to determine the cause of changes in electrical properties identified during testing.
texts.text: The first application is to detect physical damage or deterioration that requires corrective action before electrical testing. A second application is to determine the cause of changes in electrical properties identified during testing.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 5.3 LIMITATIONS
texts.text: 5.3 LIMITATIONS

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Since visual inspections are very subjective, this procedure is dependent on the experience, training, and knowledge of the technician.
texts.text: Since visual inspections are very subjective, this procedure is dependent on the experience, training, and knowledge of the technician.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Visual examination on its own does not eliminate the need for electrical tests. However, it may reveal defects that cause scrapping or repairing of a section of cable prior to electrical tests.
texts.text: Visual examination on its own does not eliminate the need for electrical tests. However, it may reveal defects that cause scrapping or repairing of a section of cable prior to electrical tests.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: If the armor is intact, inspection during spooling will only show the condition of the armor along the length of the cable. Other cable components may be examined at the end of the cable.
texts.text: If the armor is intact, inspection during spooling will only show the condition of the armor along the length of the cable. Other cable components may be examined at the end of the cable.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In some areas, inspections are performed but repairs are not normally undertaken because of severe well conditions or high operating costs.
texts.text: In some areas, inspections are performed but repairs are not normally undertaken because of severe well conditions or high operating costs.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The following procedure gives general items for consideration during inspection. For detailed methodology refer to manufacturers or repair facilities.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 5.4 PROCEDURE
texts.text: 5.4 PROCEDURE

texts.label: text
texts.orig: An initial visual inspection is made to evaluate the overall condition of the cable. Spool through the cable looking for obvious physical damage or deterioration. A decision is made to either scrap a portion of the cable or make further tests and repairs. If the decision is to repair, damaged areas should be prepared so that electrical tests can be performed.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 5.4.1 Armor
texts.text: 5.4.1 Armor

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The basic function of the armor is for mechanical protection and containment of the underlying materials. If the armor is crushed, it should be removed so that the jacket can be inspected. If the armor is separated, it should be repaired. All armor will have some degree of corrosion. The percentage of material loss and the time it was in the hole can be used to estimate the remaining useful life.

If the armor is crushed, it should be removed so that the jacket can be inspected. If the armor is separated, it should be repaired. All armor will have some degree of corrosion. The percentage of material loss and the time it was in the hole can be used to estimate the remaining useful life.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 5.4.2 Jacket
texts.text: 5.4.2 Jacket

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The function and importance of the jacket (filler) varies with the cable design. If the jacket is damaged it should be removed so that the insulation can be inspected. Hardening (embrittlement) may cause the jacket to crack during installation or removal of the cable. However, hardening will not be found from electrical tests unless there is a break in the insulation. Softening and swelling can affect the life of the cable.

However, hardening will not be found from electrical tests unless there is a break in the insulation. Softening and swelling can affect the life of the cable.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 5.4.3 Insulation Coverings
texts.text: 5.4.3 Insulation Coverings

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Insulation coverings (braids, tapes, extrusions) have the function of containing and protecting the underlying insulation. This layer may not be repairable. Damage to or hardening of this layer may require scrapping this section of cable. Discoloration is generally an indication of exposure to elevated temperature or certain well contaminants. It does not necessarily indicate that the material has deteriorated.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Lead sheath is a metallic insulation covering particularly used in H2S, gaseous, and high temperature wells. The lead may develop pin holes, splits, and embrittlement. If these occur, the function of the lead is compromised. This section of cable should be removed to restore the covering integrity.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 5.4.4 Insulation
texts.text: 5.4.4 Insulation

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Insulation is the component that determines whether a cable will pass an electrical test. If it has been damaged, it must be repaired. Hardening, softening, or swelling of this layer may require scrapping this section of cable. Softening of thermoplastics may cause the conductors to float toward the middle of the cable. This will necessitate scrapping that portion of the cable.

Hardening, softening, or swelling of this layer may require scrapping this section of cable. Softening of thermoplastics may cause the conductors to float toward the middle of the cable. This will necessitate scrapping that portion of the cable.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Insulation materials may act as a molecular sieve. This permits certain hydrocarbons to migrate through the insulation layers to the conductor surface. The polymers may also change characteristics. This gooey material may make it very difficult to install a successful splice or connection.

It does not necessarily indicate that the material has deteriorated. However, if dc tests give a high leakage conductance, discoloration may indicate a loss of insulation properties.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Polymeric materials such as Kapton may be used under the insulation and over the conductor. These should be treated the same as the insulation coverings described above.
texts.text: Polymeric materials such as Kapton may be used under the insulation and over the conductor. These should be treated the same as the insulation coverings described above.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 5.4.5 Conductors
texts.text: 5.4.5 Conductors

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Conductors are used to carry the electrical current. Cable sections with damaged conductors should be removed. Damage may be in the form of a cut, nick, break, or stretch.

In all cases, it is recommended that the insulating sleeves fit flush with the bottom of the connecting device and extend at least 1 in. past the end of the contact (see Figure 2).

texts.orig: 7.1 DESCRIPTION
texts.text: 7.1 DESCRIPTION

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Acceptance testing may be performed by the user upon receipt of new cable systems from the manufacturer. The purpose is to confirm that the cable system has not been damaged during shipping or handling, and to reveal any gross manufacturing defects. The test may also be performed on the cable system prior to installation in the well, if the unused cable system has been stored.

The test may also be performed on the cable system prior to installation in the well, if the unused cable system has been stored.

texts.orig: 7.2 APPLICATION

texts.orig: 8 Maintenance (Proof) Testing

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 8.1 DESCRIPTION
texts.text: 8.1 DESCRIPTION

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Maintenance (proof) testing consists of high voltage tests made on used cable systems prior to installation in a well. The purpose of maintenance testing is to confirm that the cable is acceptable for reuse.
texts.text: Maintenance (proof) testing consists of high voltage tests made on used cable systems prior to installation in a well. The purpose of maintenance testing is to confirm that the cable is acceptable for reuse.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 8.2 APPLICATION
texts.text: 8.2 APPLICATION

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Maintenance testing should be performed every time a cable is pulled or repaired, or has been in storage prior to reuse.
texts.text: Maintenance testing should be performed every time a cable is pulled or repaired, or has been in storage prior to reuse.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Maintenance testing consists of an Insulation Resistance (IR) Test (Section 11) followed by a dc high potential test (Section 12). The maximum test voltage for dc maintenance testing is less than the original acceptance testing level.
texts.text: Maintenance testing consists of an Insulation Resistance (IR) Test (Section 11) followed by a dc high potential test (Section 12). The maximum test voltage for dc maintenance testing is less than the original acceptance testing level.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 8.3 LIMITATIONS
texts.text: 8.3 LIMITATIONS

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A cable deteriorates when installed in a well due to environmental effects and handling. Because of this change in cable characteristics, high voltage test levels should be adjusted.
texts.text: A cable deteriorates when installed in a well due to environmental effects and handling. Because of this change in cable characteristics, high voltage test levels should be adjusted.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The minimum dc test level for determining cable performance should be the maintenance test value. The maximum dc test level should not exceed the acceptance test value.
texts.text: The minimum dc test level for determining cable performance should be the maintenance test value. The maximum dc test level should not exceed the acceptance test value.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Actual field experience should be used to determine the appropriate test level for a particular application. Prolonged or repeated application of high voltages should be avoided.

texts.orig: 9 In-Situ Testing
texts.text: 9 In-Situ Testing

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 9.1 DESCRIPTION
texts.text: 9.1 DESCRIPTION

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In-situ testing consists of low energy tests made during and after installation of the cable system in the well. These tests are intended to evaluate the in-situ condition of the electrical system in a non-destructive manner. Because low energy levels are used, these tests will generally only reveal gross defects in the overall integrity of the electrical system elements including connectors, penetrators, cable, pothead and motor. Testers include megohmmeters (Section 12), voltohmmeters, and time domain reflectometers (Section 14).

texts.orig: 9.2 APPLICATION
texts.text: 9.2 APPLICATION

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In-situ testing generally consists of system IR readings. IR tests are usually performed with a megohmmeter. Because IR readings are temperature dependent, resistance usually drops rapidly in a nonlinear manner as cable is lowered into the well.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A sudden and unanticipated drop in IR readings or low "as landed" readings may indicate system problems. Based on previous experience, it may be necessary to pull the unit and rectify the defect. However, industry experience has shown that the ESP may start and run with IR readings lower than 1 megohm.

However, this industry has had only limited success with the technology. The main advantage of a TDR is its ability to identify the depth of a gross cable defect.

texts.orig: 9.3 LIMITATIONS
texts.text: 9.3 LIMITATIONS

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The interpretation of in-situ test readings is extremely dependent on comparison with historic data in a specific field or well.
texts.text: The interpretation of in-situ test readings is extremely dependent on comparison with historic data in a specific field or well.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Some of the variables that impact IR readings include: surface temperature, bottom hole temperature, cable type, depth, pressure, fluid level, well fluids, gasses, previous exposure of the cable, termination preparation, humidity, test voltage and test procedure. Because of all the variables involved, IR readings are seldom repeatable. However, used in the context of experience they can be important indicators of changes in the system.

texts.orig: 10 Diagnostic (Fault) Testing

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 10.1 DESCRIPTION
texts.text: 10.1 DESCRIPTION

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Diagnostic (fault) testing is performed to locate faults in a cable system.
texts.text: Diagnostic (fault) testing is performed to locate faults in a cable system.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 10.2 APPLICATION
texts.text: 10.2 APPLICATION

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Diagnostic testing is performed after a cable system has failed an acceptance, maintenance (proof) test or in-situ test.
texts.text: Diagnostic testing is performed after a cable system has failed an acceptance, maintenance (proof) test or in-situ test.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Several test methods are used (Section 14). Diagnostic test methods to locate a fault are listed in order of increasing destructive capability: physical inspection, IR tests, time domain reflectometer tests, high voltage Murry loop (bridge fault locator) tests, dc high potential tests, and evaluation with a capacitive discharge instrument (thumper).

texts.orig: 11.1 DESCRIPTION
texts.text: 11.1 DESCRIPTION

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Cable system insulation resistance (IR) is measured with a dc megohmmeter which is a device that measures extremely high resistance values. The test equipment is generally compact, inexpensive and widely used by cable manufacturers and operators.
texts.text: Cable system insulation resistance (IR) is measured with a dc megohmmeter which is a device that measures extremely high resistance values. The test equipment is generally compact, inexpensive and widely used by cable manufacturers and operators.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: IR testing can be used as a quality check on the insulation of a cable system and to determine catastrophic faults and gross defects in used cable.

texts.orig: 11.3 LIMITATIONS

texts.label: text

texts.label: text

texts.orig: The insulation impedance also has an effect on the TDR measured velocity factor. Velocity factor is the ratio between the velocity of the pulse in the cable and what the velocity would be with air as insulation. The velocity factor will change as the insulation impedance changes. The impedance will change with temperature, pressure, fluid and time of exposure. Changes in the velocity factor may be used to determine deterioration of the insulation. An increase in the velocity factor will appear as a decrease in length of the cable on the TDR.
